deep.reconstruction:
CONTEXT (prev. page, §14): Euler wants to show 1+2x^3 is never a square except x=0. Theorems I/II reduce this to the equation X^3+Y^3=4Z^3. Theorem III claims that equation has no nontrivial solution. With x=a+b, y=a-b this becomes a(a^2+3b^2)=2z^3, with a even and b odd. Two cases remain: (I) a=2·cube and a^2+3b^2 a cube; (II) a=3c, a=2·9·cube and b^2+3c^2 a cube. This page finishes the proof, then begins §15.

LEMMA. If x^2+3y^2 is a cube, Euler asserts its root has the form p^2+3q^2. He then asserts x+y√-3=(p+q√-3)^3. Expanding:
(p+q√-3)^3 = p^3 + 3p^2q√-3 - 9pq^2 - 3q^3√-3.
Hence x = p^3-9pq^2 = p(p-3q)(p+3q) and y = 3p^2q-3q^3 = 3q(p-q)(p+q).

CASE I. a^2+3b^2 is a cube, so a = p(p-3q)(p+3q) and b = 3q(p^2-q^2).
- a must be 2·cube.
- p and q have opposite parity, because a^2+3b^2 is odd. Since b is odd, p^2-q^2 is odd and q is odd, so p is even. (This justification is mine.)
- Euler takes p = 2·cube = 2t^3, p+3q = r^3 and p-3q = s^3.
- Then 2p = r^3+s^3 = 4t^3: a smaller solution of the same equation.
- Infinite descent finishes the case.

CASE II. b^2+3c^2 is a cube, so b = p^3-9pq^2 and c = 3(p^2q-q^3).
- Then a = 3c = 9q(p^2-q^2) = 2·9 s^3, i.e. q(p-q)(p+q) = 2s^3.
- b is odd, so p is odd and q is even.
- Put p+q = t^3, p-q = u^3 and q = 2v^3. Then t^3-u^3 = 2q = 4v^3: again a smaller solution.
- So by descent (and Theorem II) a large solution of 2x^3+1=□ would give smaller ones, ad infinitum. Source cited: A. m. T. III p.167-169.

§15 PROBLEM: find x^3+y^3 = n z^3.
- Write n = αβγ, x = a+b, y = a-b, z = 2ν. Since x^3+y^3 = 2a(a^2+3b^2), the equation becomes a(a^2+3b^2) = 4αβγν^3.
- Set a^2+3b^2 = (p^2+3q^2)^3, so a = p(p^2-9q^2) and b = 3q(p^2-q^2).
- Take ν = fgh(p^2+3q^2). Then a = 4αβγ f^3g^3h^3 is required.
- Split the factors: p = αf^3, p+3q = 2βg^3, p-3q = 2γh^3.
- This gives p = βg^3+γh^3 and 3q = βg^3-γh^3.
- Compatibility requires αf^3 = βg^3 + γh^3.
- Conversely, any solution (f,g,h) of this ternary cubic yields x = a+b, y = a-b, z = 2fgh(p^2+3q^2) with x^3+y^3 = αβγ z^3 (identity verified below).
- Special cases: f=g=h=±1 works when α = β±γ; f=2, g=h=±1 works when 8α = β±γ.

EXAMPLE 1. α=3, β=2, γ=1 (n=6), f=g=h=1.
- p=3, q=1/3, a=24, b=80/9, so a:b = 27:10.
- Take a=27, b=10: x=37, y=17.
- Check: x+y=54 and x^2-xy+y^2=1029, so 37^3+17^3 = 54·1029 = 6·3^3·7^3 = 6·21^3.

EXAMPLE 2. α=5, β=3, γ=1 (n=15), f=1, g=-1, h=2, since 5 = -3+8.
- p=5, q=-11/3, a=-480 (Euler writes 5·96), b=-1144/9 (Euler writes 104·11/9). Both signs are flipped together, which is harmless.
- Ratio 540:143 gives x=683, y=397.
- Check: 683^3+397^3 = 381182760 = 15·294^3.

OBSERVATIO MAXIMI MOMENTI. Euler had assumed that x^2-ny^2 = (p^2-nq^2)^3 implies x+y√n = (p+q√n)^3. That would give x = p^3+3npq^2 and y = 3p^2q+nq^3. The next page gives a counterexample, 16^2-3·23^2 = (1-12)^3. Euler repairs it with a unit factor f+g√n, ff-ngg=1: units in the real quadratic order.
errors: Lemma is asserted without proof. The implication 'x^2+3y^2 cube ⇒ x+y√-3 = (p+q√-3)^3 with integer p,q' needs gcd(x,3y)=1-type hypotheses. It also needs unique factorization in Z[ω] and attention to units (ω is not a cube). This is the same gap as in Euler's Algebra proof of FLT for n=3. Euler's own closing 'Observatio' (failure for x^2-3y^2 because of units) shows the method is delicate.
Case I: concluding p=2·cube and p±3q = cubes requires the three factors to be pairwise coprime. That holds only if 3∤p. When 3|p the factors share a 3, and that subcase is not treated.
Case I: the parity claim (p even) is asserted, not derived. It follows from b=3q(p^2-q^2) being odd.
Example 1: z=56/3 corresponds to the unscaled values a=24, b=80/9. After rescaling to a=27, b=10 (x=37, y=17) the correct value is z=21, consistent with Euler's own final check 6·3^3·7^3.
Example 2: a = p(p^2-9q^2) = -480 = -5·96 and b = -1144/9. Euler drops both minus signs, which is harmless because (x,y) → (-x,-y). z (=294) is not stated.
Descent arguments omit the explicit check that the new solution is strictly smaller and nontrivial. The method is standard, but the details are left implicit.

results.what: x^3+y^3=4z^3 (equivalently 2x^3+1=□) has only trivial solutions, proved by descent via the parametrization of a^2+3b^2 = cube
results.modern_name: Rank 0 / triviality of rational points on the Fermat-type cubic x^3+y^3=4z^3 (Mordell curve y^2=x^3+...); descent in Z[ω]
results.usually_credited_to: Euler (method of Algebra 1770 for n=3); impossibility of x^3+y^3=2^k z^3 type results by Euler/Legendre

results.what: If n=αβγ and αf^3=βg^3+γh^3 has a solution, then explicit degree-9 polynomials give x^3+y^3=αβγ z^3
results.modern_name: 3-descent / 3-isogeny covering map from the diagonal cubic αX^3=βY^3+γZ^3 to X^3+Y^3=αβγZ^3 (cf. Selmer's work on ax^3+by^3+cz^3=0)
results.usually_credited_to: Classical identity often associated with 19th-c. authors (Desboves, Sylvester, Lucas) and systematized by Selmer (1951)

results.what: Recognition that x^2-ny^2 = cube does not imply x+y√n is a cube; a unit factor (Pell solution) is needed
results.modern_name: Units in real quadratic orders; ideal/element cube decomposition up to units

deep.surprise_reason: The descent for x^3+y^3=4z^3 is standard Euler material. The §15 construction is an explicit covering map from αf^3=βg^3+γh^3 to x^3+y^3=αβγz^3. Together with the remark about units breaking the cube lemma for real quadratic forms, it is a notable early anticipation of 3-descent ideas. However, the page was published in the Opera Postuma (1862) and such identities were known in the 19th century, so it is modestly rather than highly surprising.
